The tank in [the last two posts](../webgpu-ripple-tank/) moves forward in time in small fixed
steps. How small? That has to be chosen and there is a wrong answer. It is not that the
picture gets less accurate: it falls apart.

The number that decides it is the _Courant number_, $C$. It is how far a ripple travels in
one step, measured in cells. Below the tank has a plane wave coming from the paddle on
the left as before and one control: **Courant number**. The waves on the screen go at
the same speed whatever it says because the speed is set in cells a second. The slider only
changes how finely time is cut up.

Try these:

- _Start at 0.50 and move it down._ Nothing you can see changes. The same waves in more and
  smaller steps. Half the Courant number is twice the work for the same picture.
- _Move it up a little at a time._ The waves look fine for a while.
- _Keep going._ At some point a fine red and blue checkerboard starts where the waves are made,
  spreads across the tank and grows without limit. It is not a rare accident or a bug in
  one cell: every cell is doing what the rule says.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
viewof courant = {
  const ui = await import(new URL("../lib/ui.js", document.baseURI).href);
  return ui.slider({
    label: "Courant number",
    min: 0.2,
    max: 0.9,
    step: 0.01,
    value: 0.5,
    format: (v) => v.toFixed(2),
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| column: screen-inset
//| code-fold: true
//| code-summary: "Show code"
{
  // Shared WebGPU boilerplate: setup, buffers and the animation loop (lib/gpu.js)
  const gpu = await import(new URL("../lib/gpu.js", document.baseURI).href);
  const ui = await import(new URL("../lib/ui.js", document.baseURI).href);
  // The wave-tank kernels and bookkeeping shared by the wave posts (lib/wave.js)
  const wave = await import(new URL("../lib/wave.js", document.baseURI).href);

  // Controls are read live from their elements, so moving them does not restart
  // this cell.
  const courantInput = viewof courant;

  const { canvas, device, context, format } = await gpu.setup({
    width: 640,
    height: 360,
    resolution: "auto",
  });

  // The tank, in cells, and where things sit in it
  const W = 640;
  const H = 360;
  const cells = W * H;
  const beachWidth = 24; // cells of damping at each edge
  const sourceX = 28; // the paddle, just inside the beach
  const amplitude = 0.25; // height of the plane wave
  const wavelength = 16; // in cells
  const speed = 100; // wave speed, in cells a second

  // --------------------------------------------------------------- the shaders
  // The shared kernels, with the paddle on and the heights clamped (lib/wave.js)
  const stepCode = wave.stepWGSL({ source: true, clamp: true });
  const stepPipeline = wave.computePipeline(device, stepCode, "step");
  const tickPipeline = wave.computePipeline(device, stepCode, "tick");
  const showPipeline = wave.showPipeline(
    device,
    wave.showWGSL({ source: true }),
    format,
    gpu.squareLayout,
  );

  // --------------------------------------------------------------------- buffers
  // Three height arrays that take turns: one step ago, now, and the one being made
  const heights = wave.heightBuffers(gpu, device, cells);
  const clock = gpu.storageBuffer(device, new Uint32Array(1));
  const snapshot = gpu.storageBuffer(device, new Float32Array(cells));
  const params = wave.paramBlock(device);

  // Bind groups for each way the three arrays can be taking turns
  const fixed = [{ binding: 0, resource: { buffer: params.buffer } }];
  const clockEntry = { binding: 5, resource: { buffer: clock } };
  const stepGroups = wave.turnGroups(device, stepPipeline, heights, [...fixed, clockEntry], wave.stepSlots);
  const tickGroup = device.createBindGroup({
    layout: tickPipeline.getBindGroupLayout(0),
    entries: [clockEntry],
  });
  const showGroups = wave.turnGroups(device, showPipeline, heights, fixed, wave.showSlots);
  const cornerBuffer = gpu.unitSquare(device);

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------- the state
  let turn = 0; // which of the three arrays is "one step ago"
  let stepCount = 0;
  let sourceStart = 0;

  // What the chart is built from: the largest height in the tank, read back every
  // frame, and from consecutive readings how much it grew each step
  const readback = gpu.readback(device, [{ buffer: snapshot, bytes: cells * 4 }]);
  let epoch = 0; // bumped on a restart, so a read in flight is dropped
  let peak = 0;
  let previous = null; // {step, peak, C} at the last reading
  const growth = []; // {C, g}: growth of the largest height in one step
  const keep = 600;

  const [growthHost, stencilHost] = charts.children;
  const draw = ui.plotter(Plot);

  // The picture behind the limit, beside the chart: the four-neighbour stencil as a
  // diamond, and the circle a ripple covers in one step. It turns red when the circle
  // sticks out of the diamond
  function drawStencil() {
    const unit = 70;
    const size = 2 * unit * 1.25;
    const mid = size / 2;
    const limit = 1 / Math.SQRT2;
    const C = courantInput.value;
    const colour = C > limit ? "#FF4834" : "#3a9ad9";
    stencilHost.innerHTML = `<svg viewBox="0 0 ${size} ${size}" role="img"
        style="height: 240px; max-width: 100%; display: block; margin: 0 auto"
        aria-label="The four-neighbour stencil as a diamond, with a circle of radius equal to the Courant number">
      <polygon points="${mid},${mid - unit} ${mid + unit},${mid} ${mid},${mid + unit} ${mid - unit},${mid}"
        fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.7" stroke-width="2"/>
      <circle cx="${mid}" cy="${mid}" r="${unit * limit}" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"
        stroke-opacity="0.3" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/>
      <circle cx="${mid}" cy="${mid}" r="${unit * C}" fill="${colour}" fill-opacity="0.35"
        stroke="${colour}" stroke-width="2"/>
      <text x="${mid}" y="${size - 6}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"
        font-family="system-ui, sans-serif">C = ${C.toFixed(2)}${C > limit ? ": too big" : ""}</text>
    </svg>`;
  }

  // The growth each step of the worst wave the grid can hold, from the pattern of
  // alternating signs, a crest next to a trough in both directions: 1 when it is
  // safe, more when it is not
  const theory = (C) => {
    const b = 8 * C * C - 2;
    return b <= 2 ? 1 : (b + Math.sqrt(b * b - 4)) / 2;
  };
  const curve = Array.from({ length: 141 }, (_, k) => {
    const C = 0.2 + (0.7 * k) / 140;
    return { C, g: theory(C) };
  });

  function drawChart() {
    draw(growthHost, {
      height: 240,
      x: { label: "Courant number", grid: true, domain: [0.2, 0.9] },
      y: { label: "growth in one step (times)", grid: true, type: "log", domain: [0.9, 6] },
      marks: [
        Plot.ruleX([1 / Math.SQRT2], { stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.3 }),
        Plot.ruleY([1], { stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.3 }),
        Plot.line(curve, {
          x: "C",
          y: "g",
          stroke: "currentColor",
          strokeOpacity: 0.7,
          strokeDasharray: "4 3",
        }),
        Plot.dot(growth, { x: "C", y: "g", r: 2.5, fill: "#FF4834", fillOpacity: 0.7 }),
      ],
    });
  }

  function onData(buffer, step, C) {
    const u = new Float32Array(buffer);
    let top = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < cells; i++) top = Math.max(top, Math.abs(u[i]));
    peak = top;
    // Above the height of the plane wave itself the largest height is the blow-up
    // growing. After the first crests have crossed the tank, a steady wave counts too
    const steady = step - sourceStart > (W + 100) / C;
    if (previous && previous.C === C && step > previous.step) {
      const growing = previous.peak > 1 && top > previous.peak && top < 1e5;
      const holding = steady && previous.peak > 0.05 && top < 1 && previous.peak < 1;
      if (growing || holding) {
        growth.push({ C, g: (top / previous.peak) ** (1 / (step - previous.step)) });
        if (growth.length > keep) growth.shift();
      }
    }
    previous = { step, peak: top, C };
    drawChart();
  }

  // Empty the tank and start the paddle again
  function restart() {
    epoch++;
    const zeros = new Float32Array(cells);
    for (const buffer of heights) device.queue.writeBuffer(buffer, 0, zeros);
    sourceStart = stepCount;
    peak = 0;
    previous = null;
  }

  const on = (element, handler) => {
    element.addEventListener("input", handler);
    invalidation.then(() => element.removeEventListener("input", handler));
  };
  // Once the numbers have blown up there is nothing left to save: start again
  on(courantInput, () => (peak > 1e3 ? restart() : (previous = null)));
  on(courantInput, drawStencil);
  drawStencil();

  const restartButton = ui.button({ label: "Restart", onClick: restart });
  const readout = ui.readout();
  drawChart();

  let owed = 0; // steps due but not yet done
  let lastTime = null;
  let frameCount = 0;
  const groups = wave.groups(W, H);

  function frame(ms) {
    const dt = lastTime === null ? 0 : Math.min((ms - lastTime) / 1000, 0.1);
    lastTime = ms;
    const C = courantInput.value;

    // Waves travel at the chosen speed whatever the Courant number: a smaller one
    // just means more, smaller steps
    owed += (speed / C) * dt;
    let count = Math.min(Math.floor(owed), 40);
    owed = Math.min(owed - count, 1);
    // While a blow-up is growing, go a step a frame: slow enough to read it
    if (peak > 1 && peak < 1e5) count = Math.min(count, 1);

    params.write({
      width: W,
      height: H,
      ...wave.beach({ C, width: beachWidth }),
      sourceX,
      sourceStart,
      ...wave.paddle({ C, wavelength, amplitude }),
      gain: wave.heightGain,
    });

    const encoder = device.createCommandEncoder();
    const compute = encoder.beginComputePass();
    for (let s = 0; s < count; s++) {
      compute.setPipeline(stepPipeline);
      compute.setBindGroup(0, stepGroups[turn]);
      compute.dispatchWorkgroups(groups.x, groups.y);
      compute.setPipeline(tickPipeline);
      compute.setBindGroup(0, tickGroup);
      compute.dispatchWorkgroups(1);
      turn = (turn + 1) % 3;
    }
    compute.end();
    stepCount += count;

    // Read the heights back every frame this time: the blow-up is quick
    const sample = !readback.pending && count > 0;
    if (sample) {
      encoder.copyBufferToBuffer(heights[(turn + 1) % 3], 0, snapshot, 0, cells * 4);
      readback.copy(encoder);
    }

    const pass = gpu.beginRenderPass(encoder, context);
    pass.setPipeline(showPipeline);
    pass.setBindGroup(0, showGroups[turn]);
    pass.setVertexBuffer(0, cornerBuffer);
    pass.draw(6);
    pass.end();
    device.queue.submit([encoder.finish()]);

    if (sample) {
      const mine = epoch;
      const step = stepCount;
      readback.read((buffer) => {
        if (mine === epoch) onData(buffer, step, C);
      });
    }

    if (++frameCount % 6 === 0) {
      const state = peak > 1e3 ? " · unstable" : "";
      readout.textContent = `largest wave ${peak < 1e5 ? peak.toFixed(2) : "huge"}${state}`;
    }
  }

  gpu.run(invalidation, device, frame);

  // The canvas with the controls laid over its corner
  yield ui.stage(canvas, [courantInput, restartButton, readout]);
}
```

## Analysis

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| column: page
charts = {
  // An empty host; the simulation cell above draws into it as data arrives
  const ui = await import(new URL("../lib/ui.js", document.baseURI).href);
  return ui.chartHosts(["growth", "stencil"]);
}
```

How much bigger the largest wave in the tank gets in one step, against the Courant number.
The red dots are measured from the tank as you move the slider: a steady wave stays the
same size so it sits on 1 and a blow-up multiplies each step by the same number. The dashed
line is what the rule predicts for the worst case and the faint vertical line is where it
leaves 1. The growth is steep right after it: just past the line the wave is already
about a fifth bigger every step so the tank is full in a couple of hundred steps and by 0.9
the wave is four times bigger every step. The first dot or two of a blow-up sit a little
below the line because the plane wave itself is still the biggest thing in the tank. To
leave time for the dots the tank slows to a step a frame while a blow-up is growing. Beside the chart is the picture behind the limit, explained
[below](#where-the-limit-comes-from). It turns red when the circle sticks out of the diamond.

## Where the limit comes from

This was found before there were computers. In 1928, Richard Courant, Kurt Friedrichs and
Hans Lewy at Göttingen were not trying to simulate anything. They wanted to prove that
the equations of mathematical physics have solutions at all by replacing them with
grids and showing the grids converge. In doing so they noticed a limit. A cell only hears
from its neighbours each step so the numbers on the grid can only know about a
ripple that has had time to reach them. If a real ripple can get further in one step than
the grid can listen the grid is deaf to something that matters and the answer cannot
be right.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Trefethen's 13, no. 2

This is the second paper on [Nick Trefethen's list of 13 classic papers in applied
mathematics](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cme324/classics/): Courant, Friedrichs and
Lewy, 1928.
:::

The diamond beside the chart shows why. In one step a cell hears from the four cells next to it so it
can listen to a diamond one cell out along the axes. A ripple travels a circle of
radius $C$ cells in that step. The circle must fit inside the diamond.

The diamond is what the grid can hear. The coloured circle is how far a ripple gets in
a step. The dashed circle just touches the diamond's sides at $C = 1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707$
and past that the circle pokes out of the diamond and the grid is deaf. The same
number turns out to be the exact point at which the rule becomes unstable. That is
not obvious in advance and a short calculation confirms it.

## The calculation

Write any wave on the grid as a sum of waves $e^{i(k_x x + k_y y)}$ and look at how one of
them changes from step to step: it is multiplied by a number $\lambda$ every step, which
satisfies

$$\lambda + \frac{1}{\lambda} = 2 - 4C^2 \left( \sin^2\frac{k_x}{2} + \sin^2\frac{k_y}{2} \right),$$

with $k_x$ and $k_y$ in radians a cell. The wave stays the same size if $|\lambda| = 1$
which needs the right-hand side to lie between $-2$ and $2$. The worst wave is the
checkerboard, $k_x = k_y = \pi$, where the right-hand side is $2 - 8C^2$. That is at least
$-2$ only if $C \le 1/\sqrt{2}$. Past it, $\lambda$ is a real number with $|\lambda| > 1$ and
the checkerboard is multiplied by it every step. That is the dashed line in the chart and
the pattern in the tank.

## Safe is not the same as right

Stability is only the first test. Even below the limit the grid does not quite carry a
wave at the right speed. For a wave along one of the axes the step and the cell size give
a speed that is slightly low and more so the shorter the wave: for a wavelength of 8 cells
at $C = 0.5$ it is about 2% slow and for 4 cells about 8%. The tank's own waves are 16 cells
long. That is long enough that the error is small and cannot be seen. A wave of a few
cells, which the grid only just holds, is the real difficulty with any such scheme.

The result is the opposite of what you might hope for: along an axis a smaller step makes
the wave slower and so less right not more. Sixteen cells to a wavelength and a Courant
number of 0.5 is a choice that works and not one that is exact.

## Sources

- Courant, R., Friedrichs, K. and Lewy, H. (1928), "Über die partiellen
  Differenzengleichungen der mathematischen Physik", _Mathematische Annalen_ 100,
  32 to 74. English translation: _IBM Journal of Research and Development_ 11 (1967),
  215 to 234,
  [doi:10.1147/rd.112.0215](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.112.0215).
